Stratified Justification, Compositional Assurance, and Coherent Software Evolution

Section titled “Stratified Justification, Compositional Assurance, and Coherent Software Evolution”

Formal Technical Report · JIRL-TR-2026-01 · 8 November 2026

Abstract

Section titled “Abstract”

Software evolution changes premises, requirements, design choices, and the evidence used to justify them alongside program text. A dependency graph alone cannot determine whether an alternative justification survives, whether an earlier check establishes a strengthened obligation, or whether individually acceptable branch changes remain acceptable together. We introduce the Justified Intent & Refinement Ledger (JIRL), a finite mathematical model and persistent reference architecture separating material definitions, evaluation and authority, and published snapshots. Grouped positive justifications express conjunction within a reason and disjunction across reasons; inconsistency is evaluated on full derived configurations rather than incorporated into local inference guards. We prove least-fixed-point and order-independence results, characterize consistent assumption environments and their minimal labels, and establish exponential explicit-label lower bounds. Finite counterexamples refute topology-only verification boundaries, artifact-hash reuse, unverified interface-hash cutoff, and per-edge newest-version traversal. An obligation-first calculus connects joint exploration, interface compatibility, non-vacuous circular assume-guarantee reasoning, vertical simulation, and code realization. Incremental evaluation is proved equivalent to cold evaluation when complete observational projections and reuse certificates preserve the defined verdict projection. A four-phase publication protocol installs an evaluated and authorized candidate under an atomic expected-head update. Complexity analysis separates the inexpensive finite kernel from potentially dominant proof and authoring costs, while finite witness checks and a four-arm falsification protocol separate mathematical soundness from empirical evaluation of engineering utility.

1. Introduction and problem formulation

Section titled “1. Introduction and problem formulation”

Consider a service designed under the assumption that no tenant-specific rule exists. Two premises jointly justify a shared cache; a different mechanism could justify the same cache independently. A new tenant rule defeats the absence assumption. At the same time, a performance requirement is strengthened and two branches adjust different parts of a capacity budget. Tracking only modified source files leaves four engineering questions unanswered: which justification still applies, which check is now inadequate, which behavioral interaction needs joint verification, and which coherent candidate may replace the accepted design?

JIRL addresses these as four distinct boundaries:

  1. Justification under change. A conclusion may require several premises jointly and may admit several alternative derivations. Retracting one premise removes one derivation route while leaving independent routes intact. Absence assumptions vary nonmonotonically across inventory changes, whereas positive inference within a fixed candidate remains monotone.

  2. Intent versus behavioral verification. Shared rationale and shared runtime state are orthogonal relations: components linked by a common goal can execute independently, and components without direct rationale links can contend for shared resources. Requirements, contracts, state machines, and programs require explicit satisfaction and realization relations beyond graph connectivity.

  3. Persistence and coherent observation. Following the newest revision of each dependency independently can synthesize a configuration that was never evaluated together, while embedding current evidence inside its own evaluated content creates a cyclic hash dependency. Historical object identity, current evaluation evidence, and named accepted snapshots are therefore stratified.

  4. Evolution versus synthesis. An intent change ΔI\Delta IΔI rarely determines a unique implementation. The transition

    Gt+1=evolve⁡(Gt,ΔI,π,α;ω)G_{t+1} = \operatorname{evolve}(G_t, \Delta I, \pi, \alpha; \omega)Gt+1​=evolve(Gt​,ΔI,π,α;ω)

    is defined relative to an explicit interpretation and selection policy π\piπ, authority policy α\alphaα, and external checker/environment observations ω\omegaω, yielding either a published snapshot or an explicit phase diagnostic (§5.2).

1.1 Scope, assumptions, and contribution

Section titled “1.1 Scope, assumptions, and contribution”

This report specifies a mathematical model and reference architecture. The finite kernel assumes immutable content-addressed inputs, declared dependency and model horizons, trusted assurance and authority providers, collision-free content identifiers over the objects used, and a publication store supporting atomic expected-head updates with durable transition records. Proofs, finite tests, and governance judgments carry distinct assurance modes: each establishes the proposition, exercised scope, or authorization recorded in its own obligation. External deployments and data migrations are governed as separate actions outside snapshot publication.

The core contribution is the composition of four boundaries—positive support, scoped assurance, action-specific authority, and coherent persistence—connected through explicit obligations. Transformation certificates from design-maintenance systems [13], where a change is commuted through a verified derivation with an applicability argument, fit naturally as one class of obligation evidence.

1.2 Theoretical placement

Section titled “1.2 Theoretical placement”

Truth-maintenance systems motivate explicit assumption environments and nogoods, while positive provenance distinguishes joint premises from alternative derivations [1,2]. JIRL uses finite Boolean support: the meaning of a derivation step is carried by a versioned rule specification and its bound verification obligations.

Goal-oriented requirements engineering separates desired properties from system specifications and domain assumptions [3]. Axiomatic Design’s zigzagging between functional requirements and design parameters motivates mechanism-conditioned subgoals [4]: selecting a replicated storage mechanism introduces consistency and recovery obligations beyond the abstract availability goal. Design Structure Matrix (DSM) analysis exposes structural coupling to guide partitioning, while semantic compatibility is discharged by behavioral composition obligations [5].

IBIS and QOC preserve design questions, options, qualitative assessments, and selection rationale [6]. Interface automata and assume-guarantee calculi supply compositional behavioral rules [7,8], and refinement mappings connect abstract and concrete transition systems [9]. Persistent data structures and self-adjusting computation provide versioned structural sharing and from-scratch incremental consistency criteria [10,11]. JIRL connects these traditions at explicit obligations so that rationale maintenance, compositional verification, and snapshot publication share a single dependency and applicability model; Section 6 specifies an empirical protocol to test when that integration yields net engineering benefit.

2. Abstract model and stratified persistence

Section titled “2. Abstract model and stratified persistence”

2.1 Material, evaluation, authority, and snapshots

Section titled “2.1 Material, evaluation, authority, and snapshots”

A finite material is an eight-tuple

M=(C,R,J,N,O,D,RC,RO),\mathcal{M} = (C, R, J, N, O, \mathcal{D}, R_C, R_O),M=(C,R,J,N,O,D,RC​,RO​),

where CCC is the selected set of exact claim revisions, R⊆CR\subseteq CR⊆C the admitted roots, JJJ the grouped justifications, NNN the applicable nogoods, OOO the obligations, D\mathcal DD the decision records, and RC⊆CR_C\subseteq CRC​⊆C, RO⊆OR_O\subseteq ORO​⊆O the required achievements and checks. All references resolve to active members of M\mathcal MM, with at most one active revision per claim or obligation lineage. Lineages provide stable navigation across history, while snapshots select exact immutable revisions.

A claim states a commitment, assumption, absence condition, proposition, artifact description, or selection. Each justification j∈Jj \in Jj∈J and nogood n∈Nn \in Nn∈N has the form

j=(Pj,hj,ρj)with Pj⊆C,  hj∈C,Kn⊆C,j = (P_j, h_j, \rho_j) \quad \text{with } P_j \subseteq C,\; h_j \in C, \qquad K_n \subseteq C,j=(Pj​,hj​,ρj​)with Pj​⊆C,hj​∈C,Kn​⊆C,

where PjP_jPj​ is a finite conjunctive premise set, hjh_jhj​ is the consequent, and ρj\rho_jρj​ is an immutable rule specification that defines any role-sensitive premise ordering. Multiple justifications with the same consequent hjh_jhj​ represent alternative derivations. A nogood nnn declares a subset Kn⊆CK_n\subseteq CKn​⊆C that cannot co-hold in a consistent configuration; Kn=∅K_n = \emptysetKn​=∅ denotes unconditional inconsistency.

An obligation pins a subject, requested property and evidence scope, evaluator identity, and configuration. A check request binds an obligation to an exact M\mathcal MM and a consumed-environment manifest. An evaluation E\mathcal EE selects applicable check outcomes under an assurance profile. An authority decision A\mathcal AA answers an exact publication request over base snapshots, M\mathcal MM, E\mathcal EE, principal, policy, intent, interpretation, and protected-item dispositions. A snapshot S\mathcal SS binds exact references to its parent snapshots, M\mathcal MM, E\mathcal EE, and A\mathcal AA.

Arrows in the diagram show construction prerequisites; stored pointers in the assessment and snapshot strata target previously constructed objects in earlier strata. Within the middle stratum, evaluation precedes publication authorization: earlier judgment evidence may enter as a pinned evaluation input, whereas the publication authority decision A\mathcal AA refers to the completed evaluation E\mathcal EE.

2.2 Bottom-up content identity and constant-operation root resolution

Section titled “2.2 Bottom-up content identity and constant-operation root resolution”

Objects use a canonical byte encoding and domain-separated cryptographic hash, with content identifiers derived from the hashed payload. Keys are canonically sorted; arrays representing mathematical sets are sorted and duplicate-free; sequences retain semantic order; and blobs preserve exact bytes. Boundary validation checks schema conformance, content identity, reference closure, and active membership on load.

Lemma 1 (Acyclic construction). If every typed object reference points to an earlier object in a well-founded construction order, content identifiers can be computed bottom-up without self-referential hash equations.

Proof. A leaf object’s encoding contains no unresolved references, so its hash determines its identifier directly. By induction, when all earlier objects in the construction order have assigned identifiers, substituting those identifiers into the next object’s reference fields yields a complete finite byte encoding and hence a well-defined hash. Claims are constructed prior to separately stored justification records, so cycles in logical support do not induce cycles in typed object references; snapshots reference only existing parent snapshots. Any topological order of the finite typed reference graph supplies the required construction rank. □\square□

Lemma 2 (Pinned snapshot resolution). Under a store cost model counting indexed lookups, resolving a named ref to its root snapshot envelope requires O(1)O(1)O(1) store operations (one atomic ref read and one envelope fetch, with byte transfer proportional to envelope size), and subsequent traversals along exact immutable references remain isolated from concurrent ref updates; enumerating a referenced closure of kkk objects takes O(k)O(k)O(k) store operations.

Proof. The atomic ref read returns a single snapshot identifier sss, and fetching sss retrieves its immutable root envelope. Because every internal reference targets an exact content identifier and retained objects are immutable, traversal from sss accesses the same object bytes regardless of concurrent updates to the mutable named ref. □\square□

2.3 Decisions and the epistemic/governance boundary

Section titled “2.3 Decisions and the epistemic/governance boundary”

For a design question qqq, a decision record pairs each candidate option opt⁡(q,oi)\operatorname{opt}(q,o_i)opt(q,oi​) with a distinct selection proposition sel⁡(q,oi)\operatorname{sel}(q,o_i)sel(q,oi​) stating that option oio_ioi​ is chosen. Option feasibility is established by separate evidence claims bound to opt⁡(q,oi)\operatorname{opt}(q,o_i)opt(q,oi​), allowing multiple feasible options (including rejected alternatives) to remain recorded simultaneously. Qualitative assessment marks (++, +, 0, -, --) record structured trade-offs unless a quantitative utility obligation is separately specified.

A configuration WWW satisfies the at-most-one selection invariant when

∣{i:sel⁡(q,oi)∈W}∣≤1.\bigl|\{i : \operatorname{sel}(q, o_i) \in W\}\bigr| \le 1.​{i:sel(q,oi​)∈W}​≤1.

When a decision record designates a selected option, its corresponding sel⁡(q,oi)\operatorname{sel}(q,o_i)sel(q,oi​) must belong to WWW; when the active assurance profile requires the question to be resolved, exactly one selection proposition must hold:

∣{i:sel⁡(q,oi)∈W}∣=1.\bigl|\{i : \operatorname{sel}(q, o_i) \in W\}\bigr| = 1.​{i:sel(q,oi​)∈W}​=1.

Unresolved questions (000 selected options) are valid in exploratory snapshots. While the at-most-one constraint can be expressed via pairwise nogoods {sel⁡(q,oi),sel⁡(q,ok)}\{\operatorname{sel}(q, o_i), \operatorname{sel}(q, o_k)\}{sel(q,oi​),sel(q,ok​)} (i≠ki \ne ki=k), the at-least-one resolution requirement is a positive obligation: because the family of nogood-consistent sets is downward-closed (Theorem 2(i)), no set of nogoods over positive claims can exclude the empty selection while admitting a singleton selection.

Factual assessments establish empirical or analytical properties of an option, whereas option selection records a policy judgment and snapshot publication records action-specific governance authority. Authority is modeled as a coverage relation between principals and request scopes rather than a total scalar rank: two principals authorized for disjoint scopes AAA and BBB are incomparable, and replacing or retiring a protected item requires authority covering that specific disposition. Each rejected option records a human-readable reopenWhen condition for review; automated reopening, when desired, is attached as a separate query obligation with a formal predicate.

2.4 Stratified scoped absence queries

Section titled “2.4 Stratified scoped absence queries”

Let Iσ(M)I_\sigma(\mathcal M)Iσ​(M) denote the finite static material inventory under a declared inclusion scope σ\sigmaσ, and let qqq be a pinned predicate over claim metadata or payloads. Its match set is

Qq,σ(M)={c∈Iσ(M):q(c)}.Q_{q,\sigma}(\mathcal{M}) = \{c \in I_\sigma(\mathcal{M}) : q(c)\}.Qq,σ​(M)={c∈Iσ​(M):q(c)}.

A query report records the evaluated material, predicate, traversed scope, match set, and completion status. Discharging an absence claim requires a complete scan over σ\sigmaσ with Qq,σ(M)=∅Q_{q,\sigma}(\mathcal{M}) = \emptysetQq,σ​(M)=∅; a stopped scan yields an incomplete outcome, while any single matching element c∈Qq,σ(M)c \in Q_{q,\sigma}(\mathcal{M})c∈Qq,σ​(M) suffices to refute absence immediately. Because an empty match set depends on the collection membership of Iσ(M)I_\sigma(\mathcal M)Iσ​(M), subsequent insertion into σ\sigmaσ requires re-evaluation unless a narrower observational projection certifies non-interference.

Evaluation is stratified in the order: static inventory Iσ(M)→I_\sigma(\mathcal M) \toIσ​(M)→ query and check outcomes →\to→ frozen rule eligibility →\to→ warranted positive closure W(M,E)W(\mathcal M, \mathcal E)W(M,E). Queries inspect only the static material stratum and never read their own current warrant or the closure WWW being computed. Without stratification, allowing an absence claim aaa to hold iff no warranted claim satisfies PPP, while a claim ccc satisfying PPP is warranted iff aaa holds, yields

w(a)⟺¬w(a),w(a) \Longleftrightarrow \neg w(a),w(a)⟺¬w(a),

which admits no two-valued fixed point. Restricting queries to the static inventory eliminates this cycle while preserving fixed-candidate monotonicity: within a fixed (M,E)(\mathcal M, \mathcal E)(M,E), the positive closure operator is monotone (Theorem 1), whereas across distinct materials M→M′\mathcal M \to \mathcal M'M→M′, inserting a matching claim invalidates the prior empty-query evidence and retracts downstream warrant.

2.5 Reference data model

Section titled “2.5 Reference data model”

The TypeScript definitions below specify the core reference records quantified over in §§3–5. Content-addressed references Ref<K> carry a compile-time phantom brand K to prevent cross-kind substitution, while runtime boundary validation enforces schema conformance and reference closure. Process-level execution diagnostics (exit codes, signals, wall-clock timeouts) belong to checker adapter metadata outside the core semantic report.

Reference arrays represent canonical sets except for parents and bases, which are ordered duplicate-free sequences whose first element identifies the expected publication head. Within a Material, claims and obligations have unique active lineages; every root, justification endpoint, nogood member, required claim, and non-candidate obligation subject belongs to the active material, and requiredObligations is a subset of obligations. Each question has at most one active DecisionRecord, with disjoint selected and rejected option sets. An Evaluation selects at most one outcome per exact request; conflicting outcomes for the same deterministic request require explicit reconciliation, and prior basis evidence applies to a new material only when accompanied by a current reuse report.

Section titled “3.1 Positive closure and global consistency”

Define the one-step positive consequence operator

Pos⁡(U)={hj∣j∈J and Pj⊆U}.\operatorname{Pos}(U) = \{h_j \mid j \in J \text{ and } P_j \subseteq U\}.Pos(U)={hj​∣j∈J and Pj​⊆U}.

Consider first the locally guarded operator that filters each rule application against nogoods NNN:

TR(U)=R∪U∪{hj  ∣  j∈J,  Pj⊆U and no Kn⊆U∪{hj}}.T_R(U) = R \cup U \cup \bigl\{h_j \;\big|\; j \in J,\; P_j \subseteq U \text{ and no } K_n \subseteq U \cup \{h_j\}\bigr\}.TR​(U)=R∪U∪{hj​​j∈J,Pj​⊆U and no Kn​⊆U∪{hj​}}.

Proposition 1. There exist finite materials for which TRT_RTR​ is nonmonotone, parallel step evaluation activates a nogood, and no least fixed point above RRR exists.

Proof. Let

C={a,b,c},R={a},J={({a},b),  ({a},c)},N={{b,c}}.\begin{aligned} C &= \{a, b, c\}, & R &= \{a\}, \\ J &= \bigl\{(\{a\}, b),\; (\{a\}, c)\bigr\}, & N &= \bigl\{\{b, c\}\bigr\}. \end{aligned}CJ​={a,b,c},={({a},b),({a},c)},​RN​={a},={{b,c}}.​

For U={a}⊂V={a,c}U=\{a\} \subset V=\{a,c\}U={a}⊂V={a,c}, both individual conclusions pass the local guard at UUU, whereas bbb is blocked at VVV:

TR(U)={a,b,c}⊈{a,c}=TR(V).T_R(U) = \{a, b, c\} \not\subseteq \{a, c\} = T_R(V).TR​(U)={a,b,c}⊆{a,c}=TR​(V).

Evaluating TR(U)T_R(U)TR​(U) in parallel derives the forbidden pair {b,c}\{b,c\}{b,c}. The fixed points of TRT_RTR​ containing RRR are {a,b}\{a,b\}{a,b}, {a,c}\{a,c\}{a,c}, and {a,b,c}\{a,b,c\}{a,b,c}; their intersection is {a}\{a\}{a}, which is not a fixed point of TRT_RTR​, so no least fixed point above RRR exists. Serializing rule applications makes the resulting fixed point depend on evaluation order. □\square□

  • Checked generation or translation validation. A verified code generator or per-artifact translation validator establishes implements⁡(P,M)\operatorname{implements}(P,M)implements(P,M) for a restricted modeling fragment under the pinned toolchain contract.
  • Independently authored code with scoped conformance. An execution trace adapter maps concrete runtime events to actions of MMM. Property-based and replay tests establish conformance over the exercised finite trace set; exhaustive bounded model checking establishes conformance up to the declared state and input bounds; and deductive program verification establishes universal trace inclusion Traces⁡(P)⊆Traces⁡(M)\operatorname{Traces}(P)\subseteq\operatorname{Traces}(M)Traces(P)⊆Traces(M) relative to the formalized language semantics.

5. Incremental evolution and transactional publication

Section titled “5. Incremental evolution and transactional publication”

5.1 Applicability, early cutoff, and from-scratch consistency

Section titled “5.1 Applicability, early cutoff, and from-scratch consistency”

Proposition 5. Neither unchanged artifact identity nor unchanged authored interface digest suffices on its own to certify check reuse.

Proof. Let f()=0f()=0f()=0. Against obligation o1:result≥0o_1: \text{result}\ge 0o1​:result≥0, fff passes; when the obligation is strengthened to o2:result>0o_2: \text{result}>0o2​:result>0 without modifying fff‘s bytes, keying a cache solely by artifact digest falsely reuses passed. Second, let f()=1f()=1f()=1 and g()=−1g()=-1g()=−1 share the authored interface signature ()→int()\to\text{int}()→int with postcondition result≥0\text{result}\ge 0result≥0; their interface digests are identical even though ggg violates the interface contract, so interface-based cutoff requires verified provider conformance. Third, even when f1()=1f_1()=1f1​()=1 and f2()=2f_2()=2f2​()=2 both conform to result≥0\text{result}\ge 0result≥0, a consumer check testing result=1\text{result}=1result=1 distinguishes them because its observation is not factored through the coarse interface predicate. □\square□

Define incremental evaluation over a finite DAG VVV of verification units (where cyclic component dependencies are encapsulated within a single joint unit or evaluated via a fixed-point operator of proved determinism). With external inputs xxx pinned, a deterministic cold evaluator computes in topological order

rv=fv(pv(x,(ru)u∈pred⁡(v))),r_v = f_v\bigl(p_v(x, (r_u)_{u \in \operatorname{pred}(v)})\bigr),rv​=fv​(pv​(x,(ru​)u∈pred(v)​)),

where pvp_vpv​ is a complete observational projection of the inputs and predecessor results consumed by vvv (including any queried collection memberships), and fvf_vfv​ encapsulates checker identity, obligation specification, configuration, budget, assurance policy, and the semantic verdict projection.

Theorem 3. Suppose (a) the verification-unit DAG VVV, evaluator functions fvf_vfv​, and complete observational projections pvp_vpv​ are validated for the candidate input; (b) cold evaluation is deterministic and terminating; (c) each cache entry for vvv stores a prior evaluation of the identical fvf_vfv​ at a recorded projection value, or a verified reuse certificate establishes fv(pv(new))=rvcachedf_v(p_v(\text{new})) = r_v^{\text{cached}}fv​(pv​(new))=rvcached​; (d) the incremental evaluator traverses affected units in topological order and reuses rvcachedr_v^{\text{cached}}rvcached​ only when pv(new)=pv(cached)p_v(\text{new}) = p_v(\text{cached})pv​(new)=pv​(cached) or a verified reuse certificate holds; and (e) the readiness reducer is a deterministic function of exact material, unit verdicts, assurance profile, and environment. Then incremental evaluation produces the exact cold verdict vector (rv)v∈V(r_v)_{v \in V}(rv​)v∈V​ and readiness outcome. In particular, change propagation cuts off at a semantic interface whenever the new provider is proved to conform to that interface and every downstream consumer’s complete projection pvp_vpv​ factors exclusively through that interface.

Proof. We induct along a topological order of VVV. For any source unit vvv, pvp_vpv​ depends only on pinned external inputs xxx, which coincide in cold and incremental runs. For an internal unit vvv, the induction hypothesis gives equality of predecessor results (ru)u∈pred⁡(v)(r_u)_{u \in \operatorname{pred}(v)}(ru​)u∈pred(v)​, so the newly computed projection pv(new)p_v(\text{new})pv​(new) equals the cold projection. On a cache miss, incremental evaluation invokes fv(pv(new))f_v(p_v(\text{new}))fv​(pv​(new)), matching the cold result; on an equal-projection hit or certified reuse, condition (c) guarantees equality with fv(pv(new))f_v(p_v(\text{new}))fv​(pv​(new)). Feeding the identical result vector into the deterministic reducer (e) yields the identical closure, conflict set, and readiness verdict. When a provider change preserves a verified semantic interface through which a consumer’s projection pvp_vpv​ factors completely, pv(new)=pv(cached)p_v(\text{new}) = p_v(\text{cached})pv​(new)=pv​(cached) holds and propagation terminates at the interface boundary. □\square□

Each hypothesis in Theorem 3 is load-bearing: if a checker inspects unprojected implementation details, if a stochastic checker is run without a pinned random seed, or if wall-clock timeouts vary outside the modeled projection pvp_vpv​, cold and incremental runs can diverge on the unmodeled channel. When an earlier EvidenceRecord is reused via a projection or certificate check, a fresh EvidenceRecord binds the new exact CheckRequest to the earlier basis reference.

5.2 Deterministic orchestration and phase-structured outcomes

Section titled “5.2 Deterministic orchestration and phase-structured outcomes”

Given a candidate interpretation, choice policy π\piπ, authority policy α\alphaα, and recorded external checker/provider observations ω\omegaω, the orchestration reducer is deterministic. The evolution interface partitions outcomes by protocol phase:

evolve⁡(G,ΔI,π,α;ω)∈{Published⁡(S),  Halted⁡(phase,cause,evidence),PublicationIndeterminate⁡(attempt,observations)},\begin{aligned} \operatorname{evolve}(G, \Delta I, \pi, \alpha; \omega) \in \bigl\{ &\operatorname{Published}(\mathcal{S}),\; \operatorname{Halted}(\text{phase}, \text{cause}, \text{evidence}), \\ &\operatorname{PublicationIndeterminate}(\text{attempt}, \text{observations}) \bigr\}, \end{aligned}evolve(G,ΔI,π,α;ω)∈{​Published(S),Halted(phase,cause,evidence),PublicationIndeterminate(attempt,observations)},​

where phase∈{Construct,Evaluate,Authorize,Publish}\text{phase} \in \{\text{Construct}, \text{Evaluate}, \text{Authorize}, \text{Publish}\}phase∈{Construct,Evaluate,Authorize,Publish}. Distinguishing PublicationIndeterminate from Halted preserves the store boundary condition in which an atomic ref update may have succeeded before an acknowledgement or readback failure occurred.

The candidate M\mathcal MM is sealed upon entering Evaluate: any modification to claims, selections, or obligations constructs a new Material and restarts at Construct. Similarly, reconciling a stale_base conflict constructs and evaluates a new merged candidate before requesting fresh authorization against the updated parent heads.

5.3 Read skew, semantic merge, and protected changes

Section titled “5.3 Read skew, semantic merge, and protected changes”

Proposition 6. Resolving dependencies by independently selecting the newest revision of each lineage can violate both cross-claim invariants and structural acyclicity invariants.

Proof. Consider state variables (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) subject to invariant x=yx=yx=y from base (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). Branch PPP publishes (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and branch QQQ publishes (2,2)(2,2)(2,2), with timestamps ordered so P.xP.xP.x is newer than Q.xQ.xQ.x while Q.yQ.yQ.y is newer than P.yP.yP.y. Selecting the newest revision of each lineage yields (1,2)(1,2)(1,2), violating x=yx=yx=y. Similarly, for an application imposing acyclicity on a relation over vertices {p,q}\{p,q\}{p,q}, let one branch add p→qp \to qp→q and another add q→pq \to pq→p; each branch is acyclic, whereas taking the union of newest lineage revisions creates the cycle p⇆qp \leftrightarrows qp⇆q. Pinned content references in S\mathcal SS prevent both mixtures. □\square□

Lemma 5 (Publication safety). Under immutable retained objects, validated reference closure, a sound readiness reducer, an authority provider covering all modified or retired protected base items and roles, and a linearizable expected-head compare-and-swap that records durable transition receipts, every Published(S) transition installs an evaluated and authorized snapshot S\mathcal SS, concurrent pinned readers observe a single coherent snapshot, and every change to a protected base item or role is accompanied by an authorized AcceptedDisposition.

Proof. Pre-publication validation binds S\mathcal SS‘s exact material, evaluation, and parents references to those covered by A\mathcal AA, and readiness was established on those identical bytes. The atomic compare-and-swap on the named ref either aborts without mutation when the current head differs from parents[0]\text{parents}[0]parents[0] or linearizes at a single transition installing S\mathcal SS. For every protected item and role in the base snapshots (roots, requiredClaims, requiredObligations, justifications, decisions, nogoods), the base-diff check verifies either exact retention in the same role or an explicit AcceptedDisposition covered by A\mathcal AA. Pinned readers resolve S\mathcal SS in O(1)O(1)O(1) store operations by Lemma 2. □\square□

Checking protected roles as well as object existence is essential: keeping an obligation in obligations while removing it from requiredObligations, or demoting a root in roots to an ordinary claim in claims, withdraws an accepted guarantee and therefore requires an explicit AcceptedDisposition. Likewise, expected-head compare-and-swap serializes updates to a single ref, while semantic compatibility across merged branches (for example, when two branches independently consume 101010 units of a shared capacity-101010 budget x+y≤10x+y\le 10x+y≤10 from base (0,0)(0,0)(0,0)) is enforced by re-evaluating the joint obligation on the merged Material.

6.2 Authoring and maintenance cost

Section titled “6.2 Authoring and maintenance cost”

The practical adoption bottleneck for design-rationale and formal-refinement systems is the ratio of authoring and maintenance effort to diagnostic and verification value. JIRL bounds capture scope through obligation-scoped recording: claims, grouped justifications, decision records, and interference links are recorded when they feed an active verification obligation, impact query, protected authority gate, or required architectural decision record.

Obligations support three complementary assurance practices that may be combined on the same subsystem:

  • Argumentative: structured claims, grouped premises, and explicit trade-off decisions (DecisionRecord), with empirical subclaims bound to test or query evidence.
  • Contractual: explicit interface specifications and environment assumptions (such as Hoare pre/postconditions or interface automata) governing component boundaries.
  • Mechanical: automated proof, model-checking, or conformance test obligations discharging behavioral refinement and invariance properties.

With kkk denoting the number of recorded obligation and decision events, uiu_iui​ the authoring, review, and disposition cost of event iii, vvv the checker integration cost, and sss the saved debugging and rework cost, the net engineering overhead is

overhead⁡=∑i=1kui+v−s.\operatorname{overhead} = \sum_{i=1}^k u_i + v - s.overhead=i=1∑k​ui​+v−s.

Enforcing a recording budget k≤kmax⁡k \le k_{\max}k≤kmax​ bounds allocated authoring effort at the cost of leaving unrecorded subsystems outside the ledger’s coverage scope.

6.3 Epistemic limits and deployment profiles

Section titled “6.3 Epistemic limits and deployment profiles”

Formal kernel guarantees operate within three foundational boundaries: (1) adequacy of formal specifications with respect to informal human intent remains a domain-validation problem [3,12]; (2) physical interference channels outside the declared model horizon (such as unmodeled shared hardware, timing channels, or operating-system state) are invisible to model-level checks; and (3) undecidable properties of general Turing-complete programs require conservative abstraction, interactive proof, or bounded testing.

Within those boundaries, deployments can combine two evaluation strategies with optional modeling restrictions:

Deployment profile Mechanism and primary benefit Primary cost or vulnerability
A: Whole-candidate cold evaluation Re-evaluates all active requests on each candidate; minimal adapter complexity Repeated execution of expensive checks
B: Certified incremental evaluation Reuses prior outcomes via complete projections pvp_vpv​ and interface certificates (Theorem 3) Requires sound read-set tracking and provider conformance proofs
C: Restricted derivation DSL Constrains component models so code generation or translation validation discharges leaf realization Higher upfront modeling cost and restricted language expressiveness

6.4 Finite counterexamples and verification plan

Section titled “6.4 Finite counterexamples and verification plan”

Twenty-one machine-checked finite witness tests accompany this report in jirl-cold-replay.jsonl (9 records), jirl-convergence-replay.jsonl (4 records), and jirl-paper-probes.jsonl (8 records). Each witness constructs a concrete finite instance and verifies the corresponding proposition or counterexample:

  • Support and consistency witnesses (P1–P4, P10–P13, JIRL-P14–JIRL-P16): nonmonotonicity and missing least fixed point of the locally guarded operator TRT_RTR​ (Proposition 1); order-independent linear-time convergence of FMF_{\mathcal M}FM​ and FM,EF_{\mathcal M, \mathcal E}FM,E​ in the presence of multiple fixed points and cycles (Theorem 1); single-proof-tree nogood failure versus full-closure consistency (Proposition 2); downward-closed consistency and union consistency of minimal labels (Theorem 2); exponential 2n2^n2n minimal-label growth for n∈{1,…,7}n \in \{1,\dots,7\}n∈{1,…,7} yielding 128128128 minimal labels at n=7n=7n=7 (Proposition 3); checked zero-premise rules; and defeated scoped-absence roots.
  • Persistence, composition, and incremental reuse witnesses (P5–P9, JIRL-P17–JIRL-P21): acyclic reference construction and topological stratification (Lemma 1); decision selection invariants (§2.3); read-skew invariant violations and cycle creation under per-lineage newest selection (Proposition 6); safe terminal states in interface automata compatibility (§4.3); failure of artifact-digest and unverified interface-digest caching, sensitivity of consumers to unprojected provider behaviors (Proposition 5); empty-query collection dependencies; and exact agreement between cold and projection-cached incremental evaluation across 16 test configurations (Theorem 3).

Prospective implementation verification extends these finite witnesses with a property-based differential test suite that generates random finite materials (including zero-premise rules, support cycles, alternative derivations, empty nogoods, and mutating query inventories) and checks: (1) counter-worklist closure against exhaustive least-closed-set enumeration, (2) computed minimal labels against 2A2^A2A subset dynamic programming, (3) incremental evaluation verdicts against cold evaluation on identical inputs, and (4) linearizable expected-head publication under simulated concurrent writers and lost acknowledgements.

6.5 Four-arm discriminating empirical protocol

Section titled “6.5 Four-arm discriminating empirical protocol”

Testing whether JIRL’s structural invariants yield net engineering value requires comparing four capability bundles over shared software-evolution histories:

Arm Capability bundle
Arm 0: Capable baseline Versioned source and contracts, build-graph dependency tracking, automated test suites, ADRs, and scoped codebase queries
Arm 1: Flat-parent ledger Recorded claims and evidence linked by ungrouped parent edges under a fixed global conjunction/disjunction convention
Arm 2: Grouped positive support Grouped AND/OR justifications (JJJ) and obligations (OOO) without scoped absence queries or nogoods (NNN)
Arm 3: Full JIRL architecture Grouped support, explicit decision records, stratified absence queries, nogoods, projection-based reuse, and atomic snapshot publication

To isolate representation effects from authoring variance, Arms 1–3 are evaluated wherever possible by projecting the same frozen, independently authored corpus of claims and obligations into each arm’s schema; when authoring effort differs across arms, capture and maintenance time are measured explicitly.

Corpus and witness scenarios. An initial ecological pilot tracks a single subsystem history comprising roughly 30–60 claims across 5–10 evolution steps, seeded with replayable witness scenarios for: absence invalidation upon claim insertion; premise withdrawal with surviving alternative derivations; hidden shared-resource contention; acyclic protocol-order mismatch; obligation strengthening over unchanged code bytes; semantic merge violating a shared capacity budget; rejected-but-feasible design options; bounded versus universal evidence scopes; and authorized retirement of protected obligations. Multi-history confirmatory studies size their sample count via predeclared power or precision targets.

Ground truth and metrics. Before running the arms, independent domain reviewers freeze the ground-truth classification of each obligation at each evolution step, defining needs_attention whenever an obligation’s property is violated or its prior evidence ceases to apply under unchanged-input or certified-reuse rules. Recorded metrics per witness family are: invalidation precision and recall, explanation accuracy on a graded rubric of “why / what-if” queries, false guarantee assertions, detected cross-branch conflicts, checker execution cost, and human authoring/review time.

Five predeclared falsification criteria govern interpretation of the empirical results:

  • F1 — Overall architectural net benefit. If Arm 0 is non-inferior to Arm 3 on invalidation recall and explanation accuracy within predeclared margins while incurring lower total authoring and operating cost, the ledger’s added structure does not justify its overhead on that class of projects.
  • F2 — Scoped absence and nogoods. If Arm 2 is non-inferior to Arm 3 on corpora containing absence-invalidation and cross-branch constraint witnesses at lower cost, explicit absence queries and nogoods are unnecessary for that workload.
  • F3 — Conjunctive/disjunctive grouping. If Arm 1 is non-inferior to Arm 2 on premise-withdrawal and alternative-derivation witnesses, grouped hyperedges do not earn their representation cost over flat dependency links.
  • F4 — Soundness criterion. Any instance in which Arm 3 certifies a required obligation as warranted and ready using stale, inapplicable, or incomplete evidence is a soundness failure of the implementation or model horizon, evaluated independently of average productivity metrics.
  • F5 — Interference-guided scheduling. If the SCC decomposition of interferes⁡o\operatorname{interferes}_ointerfereso​ degenerates into all singletons or a single global component across representative changes, or fails to reduce verification scheduling cost relative to Arm 0, the interference-graph scheduling heuristic is rejected while retaining the underlying obligation calculus.

6.6 Conclusion

Section titled “6.6 Conclusion”

JIRL assigns each software-evolution question to a distinct mathematical boundary: positive closure D(M)D(\mathcal M)D(M) and W(M,E)W(\mathcal M, \mathcal E)W(M,E) determine which derivations reach a claim; full-closure nogood evaluation ActiveNogoods⁡\operatorname{ActiveNogoods}ActiveNogoods determines whether premises can co-hold; exact check reports record what was verified and in what scope; action-specific authority records which protected obligations and roles may change; and content-addressed snapshots pin coherent configurations across time. At the same time, our complexity bounds and counterexamples establish the exact limits of the formalism: minimal assumption labels can grow as 2n2^n2n, graph topology cannot substitute for behavioral composition proofs, and incremental cutoff requires complete observational projections. A compact reference implementation of the whole-candidate evaluator and atomic snapshot store, paired with the differential oracle and the four-arm empirical protocol, provides a direct path to testing these guarantees in practice.
